doc.title: Templates and Expressions
doc.paragraph: A template is text with values filled in. Each place a value goes is a substitution: a small script inside ${ … }, which runs each time the template is evaluated, or inside #{ … }, which runs once, when the template is compiled.
Inside an expression or script, a template string is written between grave (backtick) characters:

You will also find templates outside of scripts. Application qualifiedVariables and other conf values are templates, and the template() function holds one as a value. They all use the same substitutions; only what surrounds them differs.

section.paragraph: There are two substitution openers:

#{…} runs while the source around it is being compiled, and its result is built in as a fixed value. Since the rest of the script has not run yet, it cannot see the let and const variables of the script around it. It can call the functions the environment provides, such as generate_uuid, or eval_from_file when it is registered. Anything it does, including an error, happens when the source is compiled or the conf is loaded.
${…} runs each time the template is evaluated. When the template is part of a script, it can use the variables of the script around it.
You can also write #{…} on its own, anywhere a value can go in a script. ${…} is only valid inside a template.
Each #{…} runs once, when the script it is in is compiled. Two of them run separately, even when they hold the same text.

The openers are the two-character sequences #{ and ${. A backslash before # or $ emits a literal # or $ so the opener is not formed (the following { is ordinary text). This applies in both raw templates and backtick template strings.
In backtick template strings, normal string escapes still apply (\\, \n, \`, and so on).

An application's qualifiedVariables, and the qualifier variables of a script authorization handler, are templates that are compiled when the conf is loaded. Each time a script reads app::name (or the handler's qualifier), that compiled template is evaluated.

That gives you three moments when script can run. A #{…} ran once, when the conf was loaded, so it is a good place to build a fixed value or a function. A ${…} runs on every read, so it can use what belongs to this request, such as the current time. And when the template returns a function, that function's body runs each time you call it, for example app::makeId(), and it can still see request::. A template may mix #{…} and ${…}.

Path-like conf properties, such as file roots, modulePath, and vfsMap, work differently: they are compiled and evaluated when the conf entry is processed, so what you get is a finished string. Model on* hooks and log filter are not templates at all, but scripts, compiled at load and evaluated each time the hook runs or a log entry is written.

doc.paragraph: An expression is a value composed, recursively, of one or more values, joined by a combination of operators and parenthesized subexpressions.
Expressions are the building blocks of Adaptive Script statements, and Adaptive Framework can also use an expression on its own, anywhere a value needs to be computed.

Before moving onto Statements, it's worth noting that Expressions are quite capable of being used to compute some complicated logic by nesting expressions in a functional-looking manner. For example, take the following expression:
This expression says to add 1 to 3 if 1 is less than 2, and to add 2 to 3 otherwise. A more readable way to express this logic is using the syntactic sugar provided by statements.

section.paragraph: Values are what an expression is made of. A value can be an array, an object, a scalar literal, a call or a variable, an expression in parentheses, a template string, or a #{…} substitution.

Factors join values with zero or more mathematical operators, optionally separated with parentheses. This includes multiplication *, division /, addition +, subtraction -, exponentiation **, modulus % and unary negation -.

Doubles follow IEEE 754's default handling: 1.0 / 0.0 is Infinity and 0.0 / 0.0 is NaN (an integer divided by zero is an error). #compile strictDouble; makes IEEE 754's invalid operation and division by zero exceptions errors instead (see Language Features, Pragma).

** groups right to left (2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512). On integers it is exact: a negative exponent or a result too large for an integer is an error. A prefix operator or sign before ** needs parentheses: -2 ** 2 is a syntax error; write (-2) ** 2 or -(2 ** 2).

Both sides of an operator have the same data type. An integer and a double do not mix, so 1 + 1.0 is an error; write 1.0 + 1.0 or to_double(1) + 1.0. + also joins two strings, and only two strings: "Total: " + 3 is an error, where "Total: " + to_string(3) or concat("Total: ", 3) is what you want. Data Types and Conversion has more about this.

Comparisons join factors with zero or more relational operators, optionally separated with parentheses. This includes less than <, less than or equal to <=, greater than >, greater than or equal to >=, equal ==, not equal !=, strict equal === and not strict equal !==. Comparisons result in a boolean result when evaluated.
A comparison with NaN is false (and != true); under #compile strictDouble;, <, <=, > and >= with a NaN are an error.

The two values of a comparison have the same data type, so 1 == 1.0 is an error (Data types do not match), not false. Each data type decides how its values compare. Strings compare by code point, dates and times by the instant they name, and email addresses ignore case in the domain. Some data types, such as dnsName and rfc822Name, can be equal or not equal but have no order, so < on them is an error.

v as T asserts that a value has data type T. The result is the same value, unchanged, or an error that says how to get a T if it is something else. It never converts. as binds like a comparison operator, so a + b as integer asserts the sum; to keep going after it, use parentheses.
Logical Expressions are expressions joined together by the logical operators && (and), || (or), and ! (not).

The operands are booleans. && and || evaluate their right side only when they need it, and their result is a boolean too. A value that is not a boolean is an argument_error, so !name on a string is an error. Write the test you mean, such as name === "", or ask whether a value is truthy with boolean(name).
condition ? a : b is a when the condition is true and b when it is false. Only the one that is chosen is evaluated. The condition is a boolean, the same as for if.
A Nullish Coalescing expression joins two Logical Expressions using the ?? operator. The result is the first expression if it is not null or undefined, otherwise the result is the second expression.
?. reads a property or an index, or makes a call, only when the value on its left is not null or undefined; otherwise the result is undefined. It pairs well with ?? to supply a default:
